wording: 1. **Income.** Compute each type as for a resident. Business expenses and Werbungskosten count only if they relate to the German income.

section: Step 3: the assessment of a non-resident (§ 50(1) EStG)
wording: 2. **No personal deductions.** Special expenses, the EUR 36 lump sum, single-parent relief, child allowances, extraordinary burdens and § 35a credits do not apply (§ 50(1) sentence 4). There is no splitting. Exception under § 50(1a): mandatory contributions to a professional pension institution can qualify where membership arises from the admission required for the German professional practice. It covers EU/EEA nationals resident in the EU/EEA or Switzerland, and Swiss nationals resident in the EU or Switzerland. Contributions must directly relate to German income under § 49(1) no. 2 or 3 from that admitted practice; the deduction follows German qualifying income divided by the total positive German and foreign income from that practice. It is excluded to the extent already deducted in the residence state or exceeding the German qualifying income.
disposition: Exact prior current unit with rebound native coordinates

section: Step 3: the assessment of a non-resident (§ 50(1) EStG)
wording: 3. **Employees are the exception.** For employment income under § 49(1) no. 4, pension and health insurance contributions and the EUR 36 lump sum are allowed, for the period of the German employment and up to that employment income (§ 50(1) sentence 5). The employee lump sum (EUR 1,230, § 9a) is a Werbungskosten lump sum and applies anyway; it and the EUR 36 are cut pro rata for part-year work (§ 50(1) sentence 6).

wording: 4. **Grundfreibetrag added back.** Apply the tariff to taxable income plus EUR 12,348. For employment income, add only the part of EUR 12,348 above the employment income less allowed deductions. In effect a non-resident employee keeps the allowance on wages; a landlord or business owner does not.

section: Step 3: the assessment of a non-resident (§ 50(1) EStG)
wording: 5. **Solidarity surcharge.** Establish the assessment base under § 3 SolzG; it is not automatically the unadjusted income-tax amount. For an ordinary single assessment with no § 32d(3) or (4) tax component, it is zero when that base is at most EUR 20,350. Above that threshold, take the smaller of 5.5% of the base and 11.9% of the excess over EUR 20,350, dropping fractions of a cent (§§ 3(3), 4 SolzG). A stipulated base of EUR 20,400 gives min(EUR 1,122, EUR 5.95) = EUR 5.95. The separate § 32d(3)/(4) component and the withholding branches retain their own 5.5% treatment and do not receive this ordinary threshold/cap.

section: Step 4: the § 1(3) assessment instead
wording: The person is taxed as a resident on their German income: Grundfreibetrag, special expenses, the EUR 36 lump sum and the resident deductions apply. Income that is not subject to German tax is left out of the base but raises the rate (progression, § 32b(1) no. 5 EStG): the tax rate is found on taxable income plus that foreign income, then applied to taxable income alone. Splitting needs § 1a. Foreign capital income is a special case: § 2(5b) EStG keeps capital income under § 32d(1) out of "income" wherever the law refers to it, and whether foreign interest or dividends of a § 1(3) applicant count in the 90% test and in the progression is not settled here (see Not yet confirmed).

section: Treaty relief: exemption and refund (§ 50c EStG)
wording: - Companies: § 50d(3) denies relief to the stated extent where both conditions hold: participating or constitutionally benefited persons would not have the entitlement if they earned the income directly, and the income source has no substantial connection with the entity's economic activity. Merely receiving or passing on the income, or activity through a business operation not adequately equipped for its purpose, is not economic activity for this test. The denial does not apply to the extent the entity proves that obtaining a tax advantage was not one of the main purposes of its interposition, or where its main class of shares is substantially and regularly traded on a recognised exchange. § 42 AO remains applicable. Lack of other economic activity alone does not displace an established statutory rebuttal; neither rebuttal nor listing creates an entitlement without the other relief conditions.

section: Kapitalertragsteuer on dividends to non-residents
wording: The German company withholds 25% plus 5.5% surcharge, 26.375% in all, whoever the shareholder is. For a non-resident shareholder without a German business, that settles the German tax. The excess over the treaty rate is reclaimed from the BZSt under § 50c(3). Example: a treaty limit of 15% gives a refund of 26.375% − 15% = 11.375% of the gross dividend. For a capital-income creditor that is a corporation subject to limited liability within § 2 no. 1 KStG, § 44a(9) provides a refund of two fifths of the Kapitalertragsteuer actually withheld and remitted. This incorporates the application/procedure in § 50c(3) and (5) and the anti-abuse test and exceptions in § 50d(3); it is not an unconditional refund for every foreign company. Further statutory or treaty relief claims remain separate. The treaty rate itself depends on the treaty; see de-treaty-withholding-rates for the rates by country.

section: Foreign tax credit for residents (§ 34c and § 32d(5) EStG)
wording: - **Capital income under the flat tax (§ 32d(1)), such as foreign dividends and interest of a private investor.** § 34c does not apply (§ 34c(1) sentence 1, second half). The foreign tax is credited under § 32d(5): at most 25% of each item, and at most the German tax on the capital income. The flat tax is then (e − 4q) / 4 without church tax, where e is the capital income after the Sparer-Pauschbetrag and q the creditable foreign tax (§ 32d(1) sentence 4). Income that had no German Kapitalertragsteuer, for example through a foreign broker, is declared in the return (§ 32d(3)).

section: Example 1: Austrian resident with a German rental flat
wording: **Limited liability (default).** No personal deductions, no EUR 36 lump sum. Taxable income EUR 24,000. The tariff is applied to 24,000 + 12,348 = 36,348. z = (36,348 − 17,799) / 10,000 = 1.8549. Tax = (173.10 × 1.8549 + 2,397) × 1.8549 + 1,034.87 = 6,076.65, rounded down EUR 6,076. Below EUR 20,350, so no surcharge.
disposition: Exact prior current unit with rebound native coordinates

section: Example 1: Austrian resident with a German rental flat
wording: **§ 1(3) option.** German income is 24,000 / 26,000 = 92.3% of her total, and the Austrian income is under EUR 12,348 (Austria is in country group 1), so both tests pass. She needs a certificate from the Austrian tax office for the EUR 2,000. Taxable income 24,000 − 36 = EUR 23,964. The Austrian rent is not subject to German tax, so it raises the rate (§ 32b(1) no. 5; the EU/EEA rent exception in § 32b(1) sentence 2 covers only no. 3): tax on 23,964 + 2,000 = 25,964 is EUR 3,107, a rate of 11.9666%. Tax = 23,964 × 11.9666% = EUR 2,867. The option saves EUR 3,209.
